title: Dutch Defense Sidelines
description: A mini course focusing on White's aggressive sidelines in the Dutch Defense, like the Staunton Gambit and more. This course should be paired with any other Chessly Dutch to complete your repertoire.

r1b1kb1r/pp1p1npp/2q1p3/6B1/4p2P/8/PPPQ1.text:
Trading pieces has really helped us diminish White's pressure. 

We'll develop with ...Bc5, ...b5 and ...Bb7.

r1b1kb1r/pp1ppnpp/1q6/3Q2B1/4p2P/8/PPP2P.text:
After White grabs in the center...

We propose a trade and x-ray our e-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp1ppnpp/1qp2n2/3P2B1/4p2P/2N5/.text:
Let's see how this would look.

We trade.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1Qnpp/5p2/3P4/8/2N5/PPP3PP/R.text:
White takes.

And we recapture.

We have the bishop pair and a safe position.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1q1pp/2n2p2/8/3PN3/8/PPP1Q1P.text: It seems White can break the pin.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1q1pp/2n5/5p2/3PN3/3B4/PPP3P.text:
Because the pin isn't removed. 

Black wins.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1q1pp/5p2/8/3nN3/8/PPP1Q1PP/.text:
But the defense is illusory. 

10. Qe3 falls to ...Nxc2+. 

10. Qd3 fails to moves like ...c5 or ...Qb4, attacking b2.

r1b1kb1r/ppppQnpp/5p2/3P4/8/2N5/PPP2PPP/.text:
Simply stated, the trade of the queens results in a simplified position that Black has no trouble defending and White's anti-positional play (giving up the bishop pair, for instance) does not get any dynamic rewards.

We recapture and develop.

r1b1kb1r/ppppq1pp/2n2p2/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP.text: Because White would lose a piece.

r1bk3r/ppp1bnpp/5p2/1N1P4/8/8/PPP3PP/R3K.text: We'll play ...Kd8. A similar idea to some of the things we saw in the 3. Nc3 line.

r1bk3r/ppppbnpp/5p2/1N1P4/8/8/PPP2PPP/R3.text:
And our king holds everything together. 

We're in the endgame now, so not castling isn't a big deal. 

We'll go ...Bc5 and ...a6 to kick the knight out and we'll have a slight edge thanks to our strong dark-squared bishop.

r1bq1b1r/ppppk2p/2P1pn2/6BB/4p3/8/PPP2PP.text: We can block the check and get ready to defend our knight further next.

r1bq1bnr/ppppk2p/2P1p3/6BB/4p3/8/PPP2PPP.text: And while White does have another check, it won't achieve much.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2n1p/6pb/3P1p2/3Q4/6N1/PPP3P.text:
And now we castle. 

The knight on g3 is useless for White. It doesn't have any good squares. We control e4 and e2 cannot be used because White needs to develop through that square.

Because of our strong bishop coming to g7, we can even launch a pawn storm on the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1n1p/6pb/3P1p2/3Q4/6N1/PPP2.text:
And we castle kingside. 

In all likelihood you'll see 12. h4 going for h5. If that's the case, Black is quicker: 12...Bg7 and 13...Qf6 to threaten checkmate on b2, getting many pieces around the king to defend as well!

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppnpp/2p2n2/3P2B1/3Qp2P/2N5/.text:
For example if castling...

We propose a trade.  If White trades, we are happy. 

But if the queen goes to d2, we should trade pieces with 9...Nxd5, 10. Nxd5 cxd5 11. Qxd5 and go 11...Qc6. The benefit of trading on d5 is that we'll be able to go ...e6 to develop the bishop.

The more trades we get in, the less of an attacking game White will have.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1p1pp/2n2B2/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP3P.text:
Most likely what you will see is that White will capture the defender.

Now, very important! 

We capture away from the center. We don't want to allow Qh5+ ideas.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1p1pp/2n2n2/3P2B1/4p3/2N5/PP.text:
Instead of taking on f6 right away, pushing the d-pawn is also a common idea.

Luckily, our knight has a pretty good square on which to land.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1p1pp/5n2/3Pn1B1/3Qp3/2N5/PP.text:
If our knight is attacked, it can be moved and we'll be fine.

f7 is a great square because it's safe and it attacks the g5-bishop.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pnpp/5B2/3P4/3Qp3/2N5/PPP3P.text:
White takes.

We recapture away from the center so that we can develop our dark-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2n1p/6p1/3P1p2/3Q4/6N1/PPP3P.text:
After castling...

We have a check.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2npp/5p2/3P4/3QN3/8/PPP3PP/R.text:
You may see the capture with the knight.

And now I like 10...f5 to kick the knight out of the center. 

The idea behind our moves is that we give the pawn back, sure, but White doesn't have an attack.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2npp/5p2/3P4/4Q3/2N5/PPP3PP/.text:
White could also take on e4 with check.

We should block with the queen here and make sure White never gets an attack.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2npp/8/3P1p2/3Q4/6N1/PPP3PP/.text:
The very natural 11. Ng3 isn't what I'd call ideal placement for the knight.

Just like in the main line, ...g6 will help us develop our bishop with tempi and castle quickly. 

It's worth noting that 12. Qe3+ don't help White. We can block with the engine approved 12...Qe7 or 12...Be7.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/3P4/4p3/2N5/PPP3PP.text:
White could also try this move order.

Here, we can go into the center right away and in this variation our knight is rather stable on e5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/8/3PN3/8/PPP3PP/R2.text:
We've seen some lines with 8. Nxe4. 

Whenever an enemy piece aligns with their king, we have to be on the lookout for pins.

8...Qe7 wins here, easily.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3Pn3/4N3/8/PPP3PP/R2.text:
If White takes at this moment, we can see how comparatively our knight is more stable.

We can gain a tempo on White's knight. 

This clears the way for our quick development, which is why we have a -2 advantage.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1n1p/6p1/3P1p2/3Q4/6N1/PPP2.text:
White's most popular move now allows us to get out of the center quickly.

Check!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1npp/5p2/3P4/3QN3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
This is now the most common capture of the pawn. 

I suppose that you'll see this more often because White doesn't want to trade queens on the e-file. That would be an anti-gambit mentality, and we've already established that White is playing a gambit.

Kicking the knight out of the center and getting out pawn into ...f5 is a win for us.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1npp/5p2/3P4/4Q3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
Like I said, this isn't the most common nor is it what you should expect.

Nevertheless, you could face it and it's instructive to see why White shouldn't play it.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1npp/8/3P1p2/3Q4/6N1/PPP2PP.text:
When the knight goes to g3...

We can defend the pawn because our knight on f7 holds the rook!

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2p2/3P4/4p3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
If d5 now...

We can jump into the center to our good e5-square.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/8/3Pnp2/4N3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Because we can still get out ...f5 move in and control the e4-square.

White hasn't achieve anything out of the opening with their gambit idea. 

If 8. Ng3, 8...Bc5 is strong with pressure on f2. 9. Nxf5 falls to 9...Qf6 and 0-0 with more pressure on f2. 

Going back to c3 is a reset.

r1bqkb1r/ppppp1pp/2n2B2/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
This is also a popular option, going for the idea behind Bg5.

The best recapture is now away from the center, opening up the e7-square.

r1bqkb1r/ppppp1pp/2n2n2/3P2B1/4p3/2N5/PP.text:
d5 is now the most popular, seeking to dislodge our knight.

But e5 is our go-to square, safe and only capable of being targeted with moves like Qd4.

r1bqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/3Pn1B1/3Qp3/2N5/PP.text:
The queen can come to d4. This is the most popular idea and attacks our knight. 

6. Bxf6 would tranpose to 5. Bxf6 with d5.

Here I recommend we fall back and attack the bishop. 

No other square is safe or makes sense.

r1bqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/6B1/3npQ2/8/PPP2PP.text: We can win another pawn and should probably convert this easily!

r1bqkb1r/pppppnpp/5B2/3P4/3Qp3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
You could reasonably see this capture played now.

Recapturing away from the center is key for development.

r1bqkb1r/pppppnpp/5n2/3P2B1/3Qp2P/2N5/PP.text:
7. h4 is an interesting move and the second most popular here.

But we'll go 7...c6 with the main idea of playing 8...Qb6 and proposing a queen trade. 

In all likelihood, White won't accept this queen trade and Black still has to untangle.

r1bqkbnr/pppp3p/2P1p1p1/7Q/4p3/8/PPP1BPP.text:
If White takes on c6...

We can take the queen because the threat of checkmate has disappeared.

r1bqkbnr/pppp3p/2P1p3/7B/4p3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Against this check, we can move the king.

Our king is safe on e7.

r1bqkbnr/ppppp2p/2n3p1/3P3Q/4p3/8/PPP1BP.text:
White may think that with 5. d5 they're forcing you to move the knight. 

They may think 5...Nd4 and 6. Qe5, double attack!

But this tricky little trap attacks the d5-pawn and threatens the queen.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3Pnb2/8/6N1/PPP3PP/R2.text: If the knight goes to g3, attacking our bishop, we won't move it away.

r3kb1r/pppq2pp/5p2/3Pnb2/8/6N1/PPP3PP/R2.text:
We'll just defend! 

Development is the most important thing now. We have great pressure on White's d5-pawn, and we'll develop with normal moves like ...Bc5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1p1pp/5n2/6B1/3Pp3/2N5/PPP3P.text:
And when White develops their bishop with the intent of removing the defender, we actually don't mind this. 

We're happy if White wants to give up their bishop pair just to take material back.

In the meantime, we can develop and put pressure on d4.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/6B1/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Once again, both amateurs and masters agree that trying to remove the pawn's defender is best.

I really like 4...Nc6 here. 

My idea is that we focus on development. If White wants to give us the bishop pair, we'll be comfortable with that, but we cannot fall back in development.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/4Q1B1/3Pp3/8/PPP2P.text:
The bishop comes into g5 and puts pressure.

But our development is fast because White's queen activation was premature.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP3PP/RN.text:
You'll usually see this capture so that our e-pawn becomes isolated on e4.

We'll just recapture and make White have to work to recover the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP3PP/R1.text:
They'll usually attempt 5. Nc3 to attack it.

And we'll just defend.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
But now an aggressive player with the White pieces may try to subvert our expectations! 

This gambit opens up the queen and undermines our control of the e4-square, seeking to attract our pawn away from its stable position.

But, like I said in the introduction, I believe we are sufficiently equipped to accept this gambit. 

Our pawn does control some squares, and ...d5 can be played at the right time.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/7Q/3Pp3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.text:
White could also attemp to be trickier by giving this check.

We'll just block it.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.text:
At the master and amateur level, the move 3. Nc3 is the most popular. 

The idea is immediate pressure on e4.

The best move here is to defend the pawn with the knight. 

Recall I said we'd play ...d5 at the right time. 

Move 3 isn't the right time because White had Qh5+, piling up another attacker on d5.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/8/3Pp3/5P2/PPP3PP/RN.text:
3. f3 occurs 17% of the time. Around 118,000 times in the database. 

The point is that White wants quick development. They are playing in gambit fashion and material isn't important to them.

I suggest we just support this pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/6p1/4Q3/3Pp3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
And this may be White's idea.

But we can deal with the double attack by blocking the attack on the rook and defending e4.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp2p/6p1/7Q/3Pp3/8/PPP1BPPP/.text:
If 4. Be2, don't take the queen on h5! 

The diagonal is weak and you will be checkmated!

Instead, go for smart development and attack a pawn while covering the e5-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to our Chapter on the Staunton Gambit. 

The idea behind this gambit is to get to the Black king via the weakened h5-e8 diagonal. 

But Black has some precise ways of playing to keep the pawn and defend against the initiative. Let's see what they are!

r1bqkb1r/p1pp2pp/1pn1pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BPQ2.text:
White continues developing w/Ne2.

Other moves are also possible, but Black's plan likely won't be affected.

We'll continue by fianchettoing.

The bishop is now lined up with the white queen, so we might be able to go for some discoveries in the future.

r2qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BPQ2/.text: Most often, White castles their king.

r2qkbr1/pbpp2pp/1pn1pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BPQ2/.text:
And I suggest we proceed with ...Rg8.

Our plan is to launch a kingside pawn storm & go after White's castled king!

Black is doing very well and White will have a really difficult time dealing with the oncoming kingside pawn storm.

rnbqk2r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/2P1P3/.text:
And we'll proceed with ...b6, preparing to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

This position resembles a Gotham Dutch and the ideas are pretty similar. 

We'll go ...Bb7, ...O-O, ...d6 & can even jump the knight into e4 at the right moment.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP1B2/2N1P3/P.text:
Most often, White blocks with Nc3.

We'll continue by capturing the knight.

We're giving up the bishop pair, but forcing White to ruin their structure.

rnbqkb1r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BPQ2/.text:
Most of the time, White transposes to a normal London with 5. Nf3, but the rare & interesting 5. Qf3 is an option.

While Qf3 might look intimidating, it is merely a one move threat on the rook.

The best way to respond is ...Nc6.

We develop a minor piece and defend the rook by interposing the diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP1B2/4P3/PP3.text:
White can also grab some central space by advancing the c-pawn.

4. c4 is seen in about 6% of games.

Against this, I suggest we go ...Bb4+.

We are developing our dark-squared bishop with check and making use of the fact that White can't block with c3.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BP3/PPP.text:
White can also delay developing the king's knight by starting with 4. Bd3. 

This is seen roughly 13% of the time.

I recommend ...b6 here, preparing to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
White typically proceeds with e3.

This move adds support to d4 and opens up the light-squared bishop.

As per usual, we'll proceed with ...e6.

This move strengthens the center and opens up the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
White develops the c1-bishop to f4.

This is the signature square for the dark-squared bishop in the London.

We'll develop our king's knight to f6 & take more control over the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the London Chapter!

In this chapter, we'll learn how to deal with the infamous London System, in which White develops the bishop to f4 and sets up a solid center w/ e3 & d4.

Let's get started!

r2q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1pn1p3/3n1p2/3PP3/3B1N2/.text: If White rushes with the e4-break...

r2q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1pn1p3/5p2/3PP3/2PB1N2/P.text: And when White pushes the e-pawn...

r2q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1pn1p3/5p2/3PPn2/3B1N2/P.text:
We can respond with ...Nf4!

White is completely toast here.

r2q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1pn1pn2/3P1p2/3P4/3BPN2/.text:
White releases the tension w/cxd5.

And we'll recapture with the knight.

Regarding some typical ideas in the early middlegame, we'll place a rook on the c-file and it's often a good idea to rotate the knights back to e7 & f6.

r2q1rk1/pb1pn1pp/1p2p3/5p2/3PP3/2PB1N2/P.text:
We'll respond ...Ne7, supporting f5!

Short-term, we'll go ...Rc8, and can go for ..Ng6, with the idea to jump into f4.

r3k1r1/pbppq1pp/1pnbpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/3BPN2.text:
We'll develop our final minor piece.

Our plan is now to castle queenside and launch a kingside pawn storm!

A very complex & dynamic position. White needs to defend accurately in order not to get blown off the board.

rn1q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
White prepares to push e4 with Qe2.

We'll go ...d5, clamping down on e4.

We've now established a really solid central structure. If White plays slowly and doesn't attack our structure, we can plan to go ...Nc6, ...d6, ...Qd7 & ...e5!

rn1q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1p2p3/5p2/3P4/2PBPN2/P3.text:
White prepares to push e4 with Qe2.

It's important not to overcommit by advancing the d-pawn - this would leave us with a backward e6-pawn. 

Instead, we'll simply develop w/...Nc6.

rn1q1rk1/pb1p2pp/1p2pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/3BPN2.text:
White advances their c-pawn, looking to destabilize our solid pawn center.

We'll simply develop our knight.

No need to release the tension.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/5p2/3P4/2PBPNB1.text:
White proceeds in typical London style by building a triangle with c3.

I suggest we proceed with ...Qe7.

One of our main plans is to advance the c-pawn and follow up with ...Nc6.
This plan is made possible by the fact that the queen defends the d6-bishop.

rn1qk1r1/pbpp3p/1p1bpn2/4NpB1/3P1P2/3BP3.text:
White supports the bishop with f4.

We'll attack the bishop again w/...h6.

rn1qk1r1/pbpp4/1p1bpB1p/4Np2/3P1P2/3BP3/.text:
White has no better than to take.

We'll take on g2 with our rook!

rn1qk2r/pb1p2pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/2PP4/3BPN2/P.text:
Which is this. 

White takes space and is looking to develop the knight behind the c-pawn.

Against this, I suggest we go for ...d5 anyway.

rn1qk2r/pb1p2pp/1p1ppn2/5p2/3P4/3BPN2/PP.text:
White typically castles their king.

We'll also get our king to safety.

rn1qk2r/pb1p2pp/1p2p3/3n1p2/3P4/2NBPN2/P.text:
White goes Nc3, offering a trade.

We'll go ...Nxc3 and trade the knights.

rn1qk2r/pb1p2pp/1p2p3/5p2/3P4/2PBPN2/P4P.text:
White recaptures.

We'll continue by castling our king.

rn1qk2r/pb1p2pp/1p2pn2/3P1p2/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
White captures the d5-pawn.

We'll recapture with the knight, so that our light squared bishop always has an open diagonal.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2p1/1p1bpB1p/5p2/3P4/3BPN2/P.text: Seeing that Bh4 can be met with the aggressive ...g5, White opts for Bxf6.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2p1/1p1bpn1p/5p2/3P3B/3BPN2/.text:
White goes for Bh4, keeping the pin.

We'll advance our g-pawn!

The kingside pawn storm is coming.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2p1/1p2p3/5p1p/3Pn3/3BPNP1/P.text:
We'll jump our knight into e4!

Black has great attacking prospects.
Our plan is to go ...Qf6, ...Nc6, castle long & start a kingside attack w/...g5.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1Bpn2/5p2/3P4/3BPN2/PP.text:
Most common is to trade the bishops.

This is seen about 40% of the time.

We will, of course, recapture.

The moment White threatens e3-e4, we advance with d6-d5. Only one move by White is unique here...

Most natural is to trade the bishops.

This is seen about 24% of the time.

Positionally speaking, White trades off their active & well-placed bishop, but Black gets doubled pawns on d6/d7.

We will, of course, recapture.

The d-pawns are doubled, but we have ideas to castle, play d6-d5, Nc6, and jump into the e4 square.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/3BP3/.text:
White might decline the trade w/Ne5.

This is seen about 23% of the time and it runs into a really savage trap!

We'll push ...g5 & attack the bishop!

White now has two options...

White can decline the trade w/Ne5.

This is seen about 18% of the time.

I suggest we proceed with ...Qe7.

This innocuous looking move actually comes with a threat: If it were Black's move, Black would take the g2-pawn and g7 wouldn't hang after Rg1 Bb7.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/5p2/3P4/3BPNB1/P.text:
Another option for White is 7. Bg3.

This is seen about 8% of the time.

Bg3 is a decent option in the 6. Nbd2 variation, but here it doesn't make as much sense since White has castled.

We'll proceed by trading the bishops.

7. Bg3 is also a common response.

White keeps the tension between the bishops & is looking to trade on their own terms, as ...Bxg3 would allow White to recapture hxg3 and open the h-file.

We'll continue by castling our king.

We'll wait for White to castle & then trade, as this makes it so that White can't make use of the open h-file as there's no rook on h1.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/5pB1/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
White can also respond by moving the bishop into g5 & pinning the f6-knight.

This is seen about 8% of the time.

I suggest we attack the bishop w/...h6.

White now has a decision to make...

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P4/3BPNP1/PP.text:
White recaptures with the h-pawn.

I suggest that we advance ...h5!

rn1qk2r/pbpp3p/1p1bpn2/4NpB1/3P4/3BP3/PP.text:
White opts to capture the g-pawn.

We'll proceed with ...Rg8. 

White's bishop is attacked, but can't move due to the threats against g2!

rn1qk2r/pbpp3p/1p1bpn2/4Npp1/3P4/3BP1B1/.text:
Seeing that Bxg5 runs into a world of trouble after ...Rg8, White goes Bg3.

We'll still go after White w/...h5!

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p1bpn1p/5pp1/3P4/3BPNB1/P.text:
White moves the bishop to safety.

We'll proceed by trading the bishops.

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p1bpn2/4Nppp/3P3P/3BP1B1/.text:
If White tries to stop us with h4...

We'll capture White's knight.

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p1bpn2/5ppp/3P4/3BPNB1/PP.text:
Nf3 is a more resilient response.

Against this, we'll trade the bishops.

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p2pn1p/5pp1/3P4/3BPNP1/PP.text:
And when White recaptures...

We'll start advancing our h-pawn!

We want to rip apart White's kingside.

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p2pn2/4Bp1p/3P3p/3BP3/PPP.text:
We'll take on h4, opening the g-file.

Black is crushing here. The g-file is open, ...h3 is on the way, and Black's bishop is staring towards White's king.

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p2pn2/5p2/3P3p/3BPN2/PPP3.text:
And we'll recapture with the g-pawn.

Even with perfect defense, Black is doing very well. The b7-bishop is a beast, the queen is joining the party via Qe7-Qg7 & ...h3 is on the cards.

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p2pn2/5pN1/3P3P/3BP3/PPP2.text: And when White takes the h-pawn...

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p2pn2/5pNp/3P4/3BP1P1/PPP.text:
White captures the "free" g-pawn.

The g-pawn is irrelevant - we push h4!

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p2pn2/5pp1/3P3P/3BPN2/PPP.text: Best is for White to take the h-pawn.

rn1qk2r/pbpp4/1p2pn2/5ppp/3P4/3BPNP1/PPP.text:
White should recapture w/the f-pawn.

We'll proceed by pushing ...h4!

rn1qk3/pbpp4/1p1bpB1p/4Np2/3P1P2/3BP3/PP.text:
White plays the only legal move, Kh1.

We'll proceed by taking the bishop.

The imminent threat is ...Rd2+, a discovery to win the white queen.

rn1qk3/pbpp4/1p2pn2/5pN1/3P3r/3BP3/PPP2P.text:
We'll simply recapture with the rook.

White is in trouble! The rook, queen (via Qe7-Qg7) and bishop will soon team up to attack White's kingside.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BPN2/.text:
White's other option is to castle.

This is half as common as Nbd2.

Against O-O, I also suggest ...Bd6. 

The idea is, once again, that we are looking to trade off our dark-squared bishop, which wouldn't have great prospects on e7, for the f4-bishop.

White now has some options...

Most often, White goes for Nbd2.

This is a flexible move - White doesn't commit their king and waits for Black.

We'll offer a bishop trade w/...Bd6!

We're looking to trade off our dark-squared bishop, which wouldn't have great prospects on e7, for White's active bishop on f4.

If White is threatening e4, we should capture the dark squared bishop.

rn2k1r1/pbppq1pp/1p1bpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/3BPN.text:
White jumps the d2-knight into f3.

This prevents the ...g5 advance.

rn2k2r/pbpp2p1/1p1bpq1p/5p2/3P4/3BPN2/PP.text:
We'll recapture with the queen.

Our short-term plan in this position is to go for ...Nc6, long castling & ...g5.

Long-term, we attack White's king!

rn2k2r/pbppq1pp/1p1bpn2/4Np2/3P1B2/3BP3/.text:
White proceeds by castling their king.

We'll go for ...Rg8, preparing ...g5 and signaling our aggressive intentions!

rn2k3/pbpp1q2/1p2p1rp/3PPp1Q/8/3BP3/PPP4.text:
So we'll slide it back one square.

White is toast! There's no good way to defend against ...Rg1+ and ...Bxd5+.

rn2k3/pbpp4/1p1bpq1p/4Np1Q/3P1P2/3BP3/PP.text:
White gives a check with the queen.

We respond ...Rg6+, blocking the check and checking White's king!

rn2k3/pbpp4/1p1bpqrp/3PNp1Q/5P2/3BP3/PPP.text:
White has to block the diagonal w/d5.

The knight was threatening to capture our rook, so we'll simply eliminate it.

rn2k3/pbpp4/1p2pqrp/3PPp1Q/8/3BP3/PPP4P/.text:
White recaptures.

Our queen is under attack...

rn3rk1/pb1pq1pp/1p2pn2/2p2p2/3P4/2PBPNP1.text:
And we'll advance our c-pawn.

A complex middlegame is up ahead.

We can look to follow up with ...Nc6 and increase control over e4 w/...d5.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p1bpn2/5p2/3P4/2PBPNB1/.text:
White gets their king to safety.

Now we'll trade the bishops!

Once again, we trade now because White has castled kingside and the rook has been moved off of the h-file.

rnbqkb1r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/3P1B2/3BPN2/.text:
White develops the f1-bishop to d3.

Other moves, such as Nbd2 or c4, are possible, but they quickly transpose.

We'll continue by fianchettoing.

White now has two options...

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/3P1B2/4PN2/PPP.text:
White almost always proceeds w/e3.

This move adds support to d4 and opens up the light-squared bishop.

And we'll proceed with ...b6, preparing to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/3P1B2/5N2/PPP1.text:
White develops the c1-bishop to f4.

This is the signature square for the dark-squared bishop in the London.

As per usual, we'll proceed with ...e6.

This move strengthens the center and opens up the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
White develops the king's knight.

This move is almost as common as the move 2. Bf4 seen in study one.

We'll develop our king's knight to f6 and take more control over the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study! 

Instead of playing Bf4 on the second move, White might opt to start w/Nf3. 

This study will dive deeper into the typical London System setup which involves Nf3 + Bf4 + e3 and Bd3.

Let's take a look!

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/3P4/2PBPN2/.text:
This line should come the most natural to you, with standard development.

We'll jump the knight into the center and probably activate the queen on the light squares and unpin the knight on f6.

rn1q1rk1/pbppB1pp/1p2p3/5p2/3Pn3/2PBPN2/.text:
White will most likely trade.

And we'll recapture, of course.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2p3/5pB1/2PPn3/3BPN2.text:
We'll get the knight into the center, supported by the bishop and the pawn.

In the near future, a trade of bishops will definitely occur, but we'll have a stable position because of our control of the e4-square.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2NBPN.text:
White activates the knight to c3...

And here's an important idea.

The way to activate the queen is via the light squares here.

We would like to place the queen to g6, from which it controls e4, so that we can play ...Ne4.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/3BPN2.text:
Going for c4 definitely grabs more space.

But it shouldn't change our plans.

rn1q1rk1/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/3P4/2PBPN2.text:
The more solid approach by White is going for c3.

Once we activate our pieces, do you remember what the usual "first move" in the middlegame is?

It's taking advantage of that e4-square control and placing a knight there!

Now there's tension between the bishops.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/3BPN2/.text:
The most active approach is placing two pawns in the center.

This doesn't bother us, though.

Let's castle out of the way.

rn1qk2r/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
Once they castle...

It's time for us to get out of the way as well.

Now White has two main options.

rn2qrk1/pbppB1pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/2NBPN2/.text:
Most of the time, the bishops get traded on e7.

Let's recapture.

rn2qrk1/pbppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/2PP4/2NBPN2.text:
Continuing in a traditional manner is Re1.

White might be preparing e4.

But we won't let them.

rn3rk1/pb2q1pp/1p2p3/2ppNp2/3Pn3/2PBP3/P.text:
We'll strike in the center with ...c5 and challenge White's center.

The main ideas from now on are to activate the knight to c6 and challenge White's piece on e5.

Then, we;ll often activate the rook to c8 and play on the c-file if it opens up.

rn3rk1/pb3qpp/1pp5/3p4/3Pp3/1QN1P3/PP1N1.text:
Now it's fine to play ...c6, as we have a concrete plan on how to get the bishop out.

It's going to be ...Ba6, attacking the rook on f1.

White definitely needs to be careful as to how they continue!

rn3rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p1pp3/4Np2/3Pn3/2PBP3/P.text: They will run right into ...d6, attacking the knight right away.

rn3rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p2p3/3P4/3Pp3/2N1P3/PP1.text:
If White takes...

We'll recapture, still defending the center.

They've only improved our structure.

rn3rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p2p3/3pNp2/3Pn3/2PBP3/P.text:
White will probably use the hole in the e5-square and jump there with the knight.

We can't attack it with ...d6, but that's ok.

We have other plans.

rn3rk1/pbp1q1pp/1p6/3p4/3Pp3/1QN1P3/PP1N.text:
The idea of capturing on d5 is to play Qb3, though, with pressure on the d5-pawn.

We don't really want to play ...c6 and block our bishop...

But we'll play the amazing ...Qf7, defending the pawn.

And, what's more important, the queen and the rook together attack the pawn on f2!

White's Re1-idea hasn't paid off.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2p3/4Np2/3Pn3/2PBP3/PP.text: If White tries to get greedy and grab space now...

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPB3/2N1PN2/P.text:
If White really wants to simplify the game and trade on e4 as well, that's not a problem.

We'll simply recapture with the pawn and attack the knight on f3.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2p3/5p2/3Pn3/2PBPN2/PP.text:
If White activates the queen, the threat of capturing the knight in the center is reinitiated.

Let's hang on to our strong piece.

Although we block the bishop with this move, maintaining a "thorn" in White's position is more than sufficient to compensate for that.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2p3/8/2PPp3/2N1P3/PP1N.text:
The knight will probably maneuver back to d2...

And we'll solidify our structure with ...d5.

I'd say this line is very logical in terms of how the moves basically play themselves.

rnb1k2r/ppp1Q1pp/5b2/3p1p2/3P4/5N2/PPPN1.text: The difference is, when White captures...

rnb1k2r/ppp1q1pp/5b2/3p1p2/3P4/3B1N2/PPP.text:
White will probably block with the queen, as they have just developed the bishop to d3.

We'll capture.

The idea is that White either has to capture with the king and lose castling rights, or capture with the bishop and lose a tempo!

rnb1k2r/ppp3pp/5b2/3p1p2/3P4/5N2/PPPNBPP.text: Capturing with the bishop is more sensible.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4pq1p/5p2/3P4/P1P2N2/2P1.text:
We'll just take back with the queen.

From here on, you know the plans.

We'll castle, play ...d6 to control the center, activate the knight to d7 and the bishop to b7, probably.

rnb2rk1/ppp3pp/5b2/3p1p2/3P4/5N2/PPPNBPP.text:
Now we'll castle, with an equal position.

A lot of the times White will castle queenside here and try to quickly centralize the rooks.

Our idea should be to activate the knight to d7, and often reroute it to e4 via f6.

Our dark-squared bishop could retreat to a square like d8 and c7.

rnb4r/ppp1k1pp/5b2/3p1p2/3P4/5N2/PPPN1PP.text:
We'll recapture with the king!

We don't mind losing castling rights here, as we'll get our bishop to e6 and centralize our h-rook soon.

An equal position so far.

rnbq1rk1/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/1b1P4/2NBPN.text:
Once White castles, their knight isn't pinned anymore.

So we'll capture now.

rnbq1rk1/p3b1pp/1p2p3/2ppPp2/3P4/2PB1N2/.text:
Now we'll open up the light-squared bishop and look to activate it to a6 to possibly trade.

Our knight can go to c6 and keep pressuring White's center.

Our position feels a little bit cramped but if we find the right setup to play against White's structure, we'll be completely fine.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/4p3/3pPp2/3P4/2PB1N2/P.text:
Going for c3 strengthens White's dark-squared structure.

But we'll undermine it right away.

If White captures, their pawns will be split.

If not, we'll just keep developing on the light squares.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1b1P4/2NBPN2/.text:
Normal development by White.

We'll continue developing as well.

rnbqk2r/p1ppb1pp/1p2pn2/5pB1/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
Once White castles...

We'll get another piece into the game to control the e4-square.

White will keep developing...

And we'll go for the fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/ppp1b1pp/4p3/3pPp2/3P4/3B1N2/PPP.text:
When they develop...

First, we'll get out of the way.

rnbqk2r/ppp3pp/4pb2/3p1P2/3P4/5N2/PPPN1P.text:
Capturing on f5 or on d5 makes no difference, we'll recapture with the e-pawn either way and leave ourselves controlling the e4-square again.

The most logical continuation.

rnbqk2r/ppp3pp/4pb2/3pPp2/3P4/5N2/PPPN1P.text:
A tricky move is avoiding the trades in the center and shoving the e-pawn forward here.

Our bishop is under attack.

Let's bring it back to e7.

Now our main idea becomes chipping away at their extended structure with ...c5, and White can't jump to e5 with their knight anymore.

rnbqk2r/ppp3pp/5b2/3p1p2/3P4/3B1N2/PPPN1.text:
Now White's pieces are a little bit cramped with the knight on d2.

However, that shouldn't stop them from developing the rest of the kingside.

I recommend taking advantage of the open e-file and giving a check before White castles.

Trading queens doesn't bother us at all, as you'll see.

rnbqk2r/ppp3pp/5b2/3p1p2/3P4/5N2/PPPNQPP.text:
If White tries to be swift and give a check on e2 before we can get to do it...

We'll still block with the queen.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pb2/5p2/3PP3/5N2/PPPN1P.text:
Now White places two pawns in the center.

Capturing on e4 would only activate their knight and prove their point.

Instead, let's put more pressure on the e4-pawn and force White to capture one of the pawns!

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1b1P4/2N1PN2/P.text:
Not going for a3 is smarter by White, as we'll probably capture anyway.

This way they don't lose a tempo.

We'll take the opportunity and castle.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/1b1P4/P1N2N2/1.text:
If White goes for a3 immediately, that just goes according to our plan.

Let's take.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/3P4/P1P2N2/2P1.text:
Their pawns will be doubled.

And we'll ask the bishop on g5 a question.

Can it go to h4?

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/4pB2/5p2/3P4/5N2/PPPNPP.text:
The most popular move is to capture the knight.

That's why White played Bg5 and Nbd2; they want to remove the defender of the e4-square and play e4!

We'll recapture with the bishop.

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/4pn2/5pB1/3P4/3BPN2/PPP.text:
White will continue activating the bishop. 

The d3-square is most active.

We'll continue developing in a standard manner as well.

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/4pn2/5pB1/3P4/4PN2/PPPN.text:
Another possibility is White going for e3 instead of the more aggressive e4 approach.

This move is usually supported by c3 or c4 in the future.

We'll start activating the kingside.

Getting another piece to control the e4-square before we castle would be great.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/3P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
White going for Nc3 is similar to chapter we've seen before.

We'll immediately pin the knight, with the intention to capture.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/3P4/4PN2/PPP2.text:
Although not the most popular move amongst masters, I put e3 as the main line because it's the most natural line for development you should remember.

First, we'll unpin the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/3P4/5N2/PPPNP.text:
4.Nbd2 is actually by far the most popular move among chess masters, played 83% of the time.

However, it's not as natural as the other moves, so you may not see it as often.

The idea is to enable prospects of e4 in the future, while also leaving room for the c-pawn to move if needed.

We'll just keep developing the kingside and unpin our knight on f6.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5pB1/3P4/5N2/PPP1P.text:
This is the only position of independent value after d4 and Nf3 by White.

3. c4 or 3. g3 are covered everywhere else, and so is 3. Bf4.

We'll keep developing with ...e6 and build a strong pawn chain in the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
Instead of placing two pawns in the center, White activates the knight immediately.

This move is played 16% of the time in the Lichess Masters database.

The reason is that White probably doesn't want to commit to anything early and leaves their options open.

We'll continue with our usual setup and activate the knight to f6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this chapter of our side lines, we'll take a look at some of White's peculiar approaches on second move that abstain from the usual 2.c4 principle.

Let's take a look at 2.Nf3 setups in Study 1.

1r1qkb1r/Q1p3pp/p3bp2/2Pp1p2/1n1P4/N3P3/.text:
The only square it can move to is a7.

Once it does...

1rq1kb1r/Q1p3pp/p3bp2/2Pp1p2/1n1P4/N3P3/.text:
We'll control all the squares the queen can escape to!

Next, we'll play ...Ra8 back.

White won't be able to save the queen.

r1b1k2r/pp2q1bp/2n1p1p1/2Pp4/8/2N1Q3/PPP.text:
But we'll get the knight into the game, with prospects of ...e5 and ...d4 to get a ton of space.

Suddenly, we are the one controlling the center!

We'll castle short.

r1b1k2r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/3q1p2/1b1P4/2N1PN2/.text: If White develops with Nf3, there's a great move I want you to remember.

r1b1k2r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/3q4/1b1P1p2/2N1PN2/.text:
We'll go for the sneaky ...f4!

This move will completely disrupt White's structure around the king and the center.

If White captures, their d4-pawn becomes weak.

Next, we'll look to activate the bishop to g4 and then we can choose which way to castle. Often, it will be the queenside!

r1b2r1k/ppp3p1/2np1q1p/5p2/2BP4/2P2N2/P1.text:
So, we'll stop that.

Our plan is going to be simple; activate the bishop to b7, and get a rook to contest the e-file.

r1b2r1k/ppp3pp/2np1q2/5p2/2BP4/2P2N2/P1P.text:
One of the ideas White might try to go for is Qd2-Qg5.

This would basically force a queen trade and leave White with more active pieces and center control.

r1b2r1k/pppp2pp/2n2q2/5p2/2BP4/2P2N2/P1P.text:
White can occupy the e-file, but that's fine.

The rook is not dangerous.

Let's continue developing and defend against Ne5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2n1p3/3p4/3P4/3B1NN1/PP.text: White occupies the e-file and attacks our pawn...

r1bq1rk1/pp4pp/2nbp3/3p4/3P4/3B1NN1/PP3P.text:
And we'll improve the position of our bishop, with a balanced game.

I'd suggest developing the pieces towards the kingside/center here.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/2npp3/7Q/3PN1N1/2P5/PP.text:
White will defend with c3.

Let's kick out the other knight as well!

Slowly but surely, we are forcing White to back down, while expanding at the same time.

It seems like their attack isn't really working!

r1bq1rk1/ppp1b2p/2n1p1p1/3p3Q/3P2N1/2P3N.text:
Finally, we'll attack the queen.

Since White has chosen to place the knights on g4 and g3, there aren't really many squares for the queen apart from h3.

White will be very passive, and we'll continue going at them with ...e5.

Black is winning here!

r1bqk2r/pp2b1pp/2n1p3/2pp4/3P4/2PB1NN1/P.text:
The pawn is sufficiently defended for now, so White castles.

Before we do anything else, I suggest capturing here.

This allows us to place a rook on the c-file later if we want to.

r1bqk2r/pp2b1pp/2n1p3/3p4/3P4/3B1NN1/PP3.text:
White recaptures.

And let's castle. We should only castle once White has castled.

r1bqk2r/pppp2p1/2n2n1p/5p2/3P3B/2P1P3/P1.text:
We'll get the knight to c6.

Our main idea is to play ...d5, contest the center and open up the light-squared bishop.

We'll also castle, of course.

r2qkb1r/1Qp3pp/p3bp2/2Pp1p2/1n1P4/N3P3/P.text:
White might try to free up the bishop on f1, but it doesn't help.

We'll attack the queen.

r2qkb1r/pQp3pp/2n1bp2/3p1p2/2PP4/4P3/PP3.text:
If White captures, they're already lost without even knowing it.

We'll play the amazing ...Nb4!

We place the knight on the b4-square and look to fork White's king and rook.

This move blocks the queen's retreating path, which will be extremely useful in the near future, as you'll see.

r2qkb1r/pQp3pp/4bp2/3p1p2/1nPP4/N3P3/PP3.text:
The most logical way of defending against ...Nc2 is Na3.

If you remember this move, you'll realize that White's queen is suddenly trapped on b7!

All the squares around it are controlled by our pieces.

r3kb1r/pppq2pp/2n1bp2/3p1p2/3P4/3BPQN1/P.text: If White plays Ng3, we are ready.

r3kb1r/pppq3p/2n1bpp1/3p1p2/3P4/3BPQN1/P.text: Now we can play ...g6 and castle queenside soon.

rn1q1rk1/ppp3pp/5p2/3N4/3P1p2/P3P3/1P3PP.text:
If White decides to capture in the center...

We'll just take.

There is one thing we need to be careful about, however.

rn1q1rk1/ppp3pp/5p2/3b1p2/1b1P4/P1N1P3/1.text:
If White attacks our bishop, there is no point in retreating anymore and letting White get the momentum.

Let's capture.

rn1q1rk1/ppp3pp/5p2/3b1p2/3P4/P1N1P3/1P3.text:
White will recapture with the knight, attacking the bishop again.

But we have that one move that changes their plans a little bit.

Let's challenge the e3-pawn!

In this instance, there is no pressure on d4, so White could even capture.

rn1qk2r/ppp3pp/5p2/3b1p2/1b1P4/2N1P3/PP2.text:
If White wants to preserve the pressure on the center, they will have to support the knight with Ne2.

Let's castle out of the way.

rn1qkb1r/ppp3pp/4bp2/3P1p2/3P4/4P3/PP3PP.text:
If White captures in the center...

We'll recapture with the bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp3pp/4bp2/3p1p2/2PP4/1Q2P3/PP.text:
Another way of continuing the attack on the d5-pawn is Qb3.

Our b7-pawn is also under attack.

Let's set a trap for White!

rn1qkb1r/ppp3pp/4bp2/3p1p2/3P4/3BPQ2/PPP.text:
White might continue the pressure with Qf3.

Going for ...g6 might be too weakening for our structure, but here's another idea behind ...Be6.

We'll play ...Qd7 and defend the f5-pawn.

rn1qkb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3b1p2/3P4/2N1P3/PP3P.text:
Nc3 attacks it, but we already know how to respond to that.

Let's pin the knight.

rn1qr1k1/ppp3pp/5p2/3b4/3P1P2/P1N5/1P3PP.text:
The e-file suddenly opens up and we can deliver a check on it.

White will probably have to block with the bishop, which is in itself uncomfortable, as the g2-pawn would hang.

In the future, I like playing ...c6 to control the d5-square if White wants to push d5 and activating the knight on the queenside.

rn2kb1r/pppq2pp/4bp2/3p1p2/3P4/3BPQ2/PPP.text:
White might continue developing with Ne2, trying to go for Ng3 and add another attacker to the pawn.

And we'll go for ...Nc6, aiming to castle long!

rn3r1k/ppp3pp/5p2/3q4/3P1p2/P3P3/1P3PPP/.text:
Simply sliding the king out of the way saves our queen.

Our plan is, if allowed, to capture on e3 and then develop normally with ...Nc6 and get the rooks to the center.

rn3rk1/pbppq1pp/1p2p3/4Pp2/3P4/2PB1N2/P1.text:
White does have some space, but we have got a pretty comfortable position.

A good idea would be to chip away at White's structure with ...c5, activate the knight to c6 and get the a-rook into the game.

rn3rk1/ppp3pp/5p2/3q4/3P1p2/P3P3/1P3PPP/.text:
White might play Rc1 and try to go for Bc4!

Always be on the lookout for tactics on the f8-a2 diagonal when you move your f-pawn as Black.

rnb1k2r/p1ppq1pp/1p2p3/4Pp2/3P4/2PB1N2/P.text:
White continues developing...

And so will we.

rnb1k2r/pp2q1bp/4p1p1/2Pp4/8/2N1Q3/PPP2P.text: White could take the free pawn...

rnb1k2r/ppp1q1bp/4p1p1/3p4/3P4/2N1Q3/PPP.text:
The most natural retreating square is c3.

A very aggressive approach by us is trying to take advantage of the fact that White's c-pawn is blocked and chip away at their central structure.

rnb1k2r/ppp3pp/5p2/3q1p2/1b1P4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
They might go for e3, trying to open up the light-squared bishop.

But we'll just keep developing.

I like ...Nc6 here, not blocking the bishop with ...Nd7 and maintaining some pressure in the center.

rnb1k2r/pppp2p1/4Pq1p/8/1b1P4/2N5/PPP1PP.text:
If White gets greedy and captures, we have an inbetween move.

Let's castle with pressure on f2.

Having already weakened their kingside with g4, White has to defend against this as well.

rnb1k2r/pppp2pp/4pq2/4Pp2/1b1P4/2N5/PPP2.text:
A more direct approach by White is shoving the e-pawn forward and attacking our queen.

I recommend taking here with check and doubling White's c-pawns.

rnb1k2r/pppp2pp/4pq2/4Pp2/3P4/2P5/P1P2PP.text:
They will take back...

And let's retreat to e7.

From this square, our queen is still active but safe.

rnb1k2r/pppp2pp/4pq2/5P2/1b1P4/2N5/PPP2P.text:
If White chooses to capture on f5, we don't need to recapture right away.

We can actually castle out of the way here.

White can't keep taking because of the weak f2-pawn.

rnb1k2r/ppppq1bp/4p1p1/8/3PN3/4Q3/PPP2PP.text:
Once it does...

We'll place a pawn in the center with tempo.

rnb1k2r/ppppq1pp/4p3/4Pp2/3P4/2P2N2/P1P2.text:
A natural response by White, and we'll respond naturally as well.

Let's open up the b7-square for our bishop.

rnb1k2r/ppppq2p/4pbpQ/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/2.text:
If White doesn't capture our bishop and castles, our plan for the future is easy.

We'll kick out the queen and then finally get some pawns to the center so that White can feel our presence!

First, their queen has to move.

rnb1kb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3q1p2/3P4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
It will probably get attacked immediately...

But we'll pin the knight while developing the bishop.

White can't capture the queen, of course.

rnb1kb1r/pppp2pp/4pq2/5p2/3PP3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
Once e4 comes...

We'll do the same thing White did to us.

We'll restrict the piece that controls the e4-square!

rnb2r1k/pppp2pp/5q2/5p2/2BP4/2P2N2/P1P2P.text:
White will castle and disallow any checks on the e-file...

And we'll keep developing.

The most natural is ...Nc6, with ideas of ...d6 to open up our bishop.

rnb2rk1/ppp3p1/4Pq1p/3p4/1b1P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
And we'll place a pawn in the center with ...d5.

The e6-pawn isn't going anywhere; we'll capture it with the bishop.

After that, getting the knight into the game, probably via...Nd7, would be great.

rnb2rk1/pppp2p1/4Pq1p/8/1b1P4/2N2N2/PPP1.text: The most natural defense is Nf3.

rnb2rk1/pppp2pp/4pq2/5P2/1b1P4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
They will probably activate the knight and reintroduce the threat of capturing on e6.

We'll finish the job we started on the queenside...

rnb2rk1/pppp2pp/4pq2/5P2/3P4/2P2N2/P1P2P.text:
And once White recaptures, we'll finally take back.

Now the e-file is open, but so is the g8-a2 diagonal, on which our king stands.

rnb2rk1/pppp2pp/5q2/5p2/2BP4/2P2N2/P1P2P.text:
White often uses that to their advantage to develop a piece with tempo.

Let's get out of the way.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/3pp3/7Q/3PN1N1/8/PPP2P.text:
Once it retreats, probably to g4...

I suggest we simply keep developing and pressure the center.

Our rook and bishop together nicely control the f6-square.

rnbq1rk1/ppppb1pp/4p3/4N2Q/3PN3/8/PPP2PP.text:
The queen lands on the active h5-square and eyes our king.

But that's fine, as there aren't any threats at the moment.

And there won't be, as far as we are concerned!

We'll kick out the knight first.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/4p3/2pp4/3P4/2PB1NN1/PP3.text:
So White will probably choose to defend the d4-pawn.

We'll keep going at it.

rnbqk2r/ppp1b1pp/4p3/3p4/3P4/3B1NN1/PPP2.text:
White retreats to g3, which only allows us to keep expanding.

Striking in the center and challenging White's.

Capturing here only activates our bishop...

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pB1p/5P2/1b1P4/2N5/PPP1.text:
If White takes, we'll recapture with the queen and gambit a pawn but reach a very active and healthy position.

Our queen is eyeing the f2-pawn behind the f5-pawn...

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/4pn1p/5P2/1b1P3B/2N5/PPP.text:
If White doesn't bite and chooses to retreat...

Then we'll capture, with a concrete idea in mind.

If White isn't careful, we'll suddenly play ...g5 and ...f4 and trap their bishop!

This is another idea of ...h6.

rnbqk2r/pppp2p1/5n1p/5p2/1b1P3B/2N1P3/PP.text:
7.e3 grabs control of the f4-square and disallows us from trapping the bishop.

That's fine, we'll still double White's pawns and keep developing.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pb2/7Q/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Another aggressive approach by White is giving a check here immediately and provoking ...g6.

We have to block.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pb2/8/3PN3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
The most traditional one being Nf3, simply developing on the kingside.

I recommend retreating here and preserving the bishop pair.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5PB1/1b1P4/2N5/PPP1.text:
And they probably will.

I recommend attacking the bishop here rather than capturing.

rnbqk2r/pppp3p/4pbpQ/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R3.text:
White's idea is to move the queen to h6 and prevent us from castling.

This looks uncomfortable, but is completely fine.

Just remember to control the g7-square and look to retreat the bishop to g7.

Which we'll start doing

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/4p3/4N3/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
If White really wants to play aggressively and threaten Qh5...

Let them come!

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/4p3/8/3PN3/3B1N2/PPP2PP.text:
If White isn't that aggressive and simply continues developing, that's fine.

They won't get in any trouble, but so won't we.

Let's grab space in the center with tempo.

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/4pB2/8/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
So, White will probably capture, leaving their knight in the center.

After we take back, White has multiple options.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3P1p2/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
The most challenging line is White capturing in the center.

We are forced to recapture with the queen and get it to the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3p1p2/2PP4/4P3/PP3PP.text:
We also have to be ready for c4 now, as it can come at any moment.

As in the 5.Bd3 line, we'll defend the pawn with ...Be6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/5p2/3p1p2/3P4/3BP3/PPP2P.text:
White developing the bishop to d3 is not an issue.

We can just continue activating our pieces.

I like ...Be6 here, as it keeps vision on both the f5- and the d5-pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pB2/5p2/3P4/2N5/PPP1PP.text:
White could also capture here and then go for e4.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/3P2P1/2N5/PPP.text:
A move played about 5% of the time is g4.

White wants to make us relinquish control of e4 and place a pawn there.

Capturing here is not recommended.

Let's pin White's knight instead!

We don't mind them taking.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5pB1/3PP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
By far the most popular move, played about 90% of the time, is e4.

That's what White was going for anyway; central control.

Let's not give it to them.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/6B1/3PN3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
If the knight recaptures and puts pressure on our pinned knight, we aren't scared.

We've always got the bishop to unpin and defend.

Now the threat of ...Nxe4 is introduced.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5p2/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
If White tries the usual approach with placing two pawns in the center, it's important to realize there's not a knight on c3 yet.

So we can go for the immediate d5!

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5p2/5p2/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP.text:
A more peaceful approach is to go for e3, strengthening the central structure and opening up the bishop.

Let's play in the center with ...d5.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5B2/5p2/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
White takes.

Let's recapture with the e-pawn and open up our bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5pB1/3P4/2N5/PPP1P.text:
Our knight controls the e4-square.

So, White often wants to get rid of it!

Let's open up the bishop.

Although we have to play this move in order to develop, it gives White the chance to push e4 immediately.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P4/2N5/PPP1PPPP.text:
Another move White could play is Nc3 here.

Although blocking the c-pawn, the idea is to try and achieve an early e4 or g4, as you'll see.

We'll continue in our usual style.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5pB1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/.text:
Definitely an aggressive approach is White going for Bg5 immediately.

The idea is to remove our knight from the f6-square and try to disrupt our structure.

We'll let them do it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the second study of our side lines, we'll take a look at White playing Nc3 on move 2 instead of c4, trying to go for an early e4 or g4.

Another possibility is the immediate Bg5, looking to capture our knight on f6 when it arrives there.

We need to be prepared for both!

r1b1k1nr/ppp1q1pp/3b4/3pNP2/8/4Q3/PPP1PP.text: So, White will probably capture themselves first.

r1b1k1nr/ppp1q1pp/8/3pbP2/8/4Q3/PPP1PP1P.text:
Let's avoid a queen trade and recapture with the bishop.

Next, we'll develop normally and castle.

r1b1k1nr/ppp3pp/3b4/3pnP2/5P1q/4Q3/PPP1P.text:
White moves the king out of the way.

We are not done with creating threats, though.

Let's attack the queen with d4.

If White wants to keep the pin and plays Qe4, they jump right into ...Nf6.

r1b1k1nr/ppp3pp/3b4/4nP2/3Q1P1q/8/PPP1P2.text:
So, White will most likely capture on d4.

However, that allows for a great move by us.

r1b1k1nr/ppp3pp/3b4/5P2/3Q1Pnq/8/PPP1P2P.text:
We'll move the knight to g4, with the threat of ...Nf2+.

The best way for White to stop it is to play Nf3 followed by Qg1, which is very passive.

Keep in mind that the f5-pawn is still hanging.

Believe it or not, Black is winning here!

r1bqk1nr/ppp1b1pp/2n5/3p1P2/8/4Q2B/PPP1P.text: White might try to hold on to the f5-pawn.

r1bqk1nr/ppp3pp/3b4/3pnP2/5P2/4Q3/PPP1P2.text:
If White goes for f4, this is already a mistake.

Yes, our knight can't move, but remember what I said about the diagonal that opens if White moves the f-pawn?

Let's give a check from the h4-square.

r1bqk1nr/ppp3pp/3b4/3pnP2/8/4QN2/PPP1PP1.text:
A smarter move than f4 is Nf3, adding an attacker to our pinned knight.

We'll unpin and defend.

Now we are threatening to capture on f3 and simplify the position.

r1bqk1r1/ppp2nQp/3b1n2/3p1P2/8/2N5/PPPBP.text:
Oops!

Their queen suddenly gets trapped on the g7-square, with no squares to retreat to.

We'll win the queen on the next move, and soon the game.

r1bqk2r/ppp1b1pp/2n2n2/3p1P2/8/4Q2B/PPP1.text:
But that's fine, we'll just get the knight out and castle on the next move.

Our position is very strong with a lead in development, while White has played with the queen too many times and hasn't developed enough pieces!

There is still chess to be played, however.

r1bqk2r/ppp2nQp/3b1n2/3p1P2/8/2N5/PPPBPP.text: If White is greedy, thinking they've won a pawn...

r1bqkb1r/ppp2npp/5n2/3p1P2/8/2N3Q1/PPPBP.text:
Developing the bishop anywhere but d2 might be risky.

This allows us to get the bishop out with tempo, though!

You might notice that our g7-pawn is hanging.

Let's see what happens if White blunders and takes it.

r1bqkbnr/pp2p1pp/2n5/2pp1pP1/3P4/2P2N2/P.text: The most logical is for White to activate the knight and defend the pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pp4pp/2n1p3/2pp1pP1/3P4/2P2N2/P.text:
We'll continue with ...e6, strengthening the center.

I recommend activating the kingside knight to g6 via e7, that way it can pressure the bishop if it arrives on f4.

Our bishop, on the other hand, will develop to the natural d6-square.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2npp/8/3p1P2/8/2N3Q1/PPP1PP1.text:
White can't threaten anything anymore, so they'll probably keep developing.

Having moved the g-pawn, it's smarter for them to get the queenside pieces out and castle long quickly.

Let's keep activating our own pieces.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/3p1P2/8/4Q3/PPP1PP1P.text:
If White retreats and gives a check...

We'll block with the bishop.

Our plan stays the same; activate the knight, capture on f5 and castle.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/3pPP2/8/3Q4/PPP1PP1P.text:
So, White will most likely get greedy and capture on f5.

We'll go ahead and get back one of the pawns with tempo on the queen.

From here on, White has a couple of options.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pnP2/8/4Q3/PPP1PP1P/R.text:
Some players will pin your knight on e5, which definitely looks dangerous.

The threat is f4, winning the knight.

But we're good!

We'll develop the bishop and defend the knight in the center.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pnP2/8/6Q1/PPP1PP1P/R.text:
White might go Qg3 here, putting pressure on the knight while leaving space for the e-pawn to move.

Also, we can't play ...Bd6, as that would hang our g7-pawn!

I know the f7-square isn't really where the knight finds itself in most positions, but we are completely fine.

rn1qk2r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1b2/1bPP4/2N5/PP2P.text:
We'll simply pin it.

You've already seen this idea before.

Next, we'll get our knight to c6 and castle.

rn1qkb1r/ppp1p1pp/5n2/3p1b2/2PP4/8/PP2PP.text:
The most critical is for White to challenge the center with c4.

If we capture, we'll lose the b7-pawn and the rook.

So I recommend simply defending the center and letting White capture if they want to.

Our bishop is also ready to get out.

rn1qkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1b2/2PP4/2N5/PP2P.text: If White develops the knight and adds another attacker to the center...

rn1qkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p1b2/3P4/8/PPP1PPBP.text:
White might use the g-pawn moving to g4 and fianchetto the bishop...

But we'll just keep developing.

We've already got a lead in development with Black.

rnbqk2r/ppp1b1pp/4pn2/3p1pB1/3P4/2NQ4/PP.text:
And we'll unpin the knight.

Our plan should be the following:

After we castle, we'll play ...Nd7 and go for ...c5 to strike in the center!

The idea is, that if the c-file opens up, we can use a rook in the future to attack on it.

White's king is on c1, after all.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1p1pp/5n2/3p1pB1/3P4/2NQ4/PP.text:
If White tries to pressure our knight, that's fine.

We have more defenders!

We'll play ...e6 and open up our dark-squared bishop.

Pinning our knight is okay here as we are planning to play ...Be7 anyway.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4p3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NQ1N2/P.text:
Let's shove our knight into the center, Stonewall style!

Next, we'll play ...c6 to solidify the center, get our bishop out and castle.

Our position is very solid.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NQ1N2/P.text:
Both knights out.

Before continuing development...

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1pB1/3P4/2NQ4/PPP.text: White castles before activating the kingside...

rnbqkbnr/pp2p1pp/8/2pp1pP1/3P4/2P5/PP2PP.text:
So they'll most likely defend the pawn with c3.

But we'll continue piling pressure.

The knight on c6 is another attacker on the d4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pp4pp/8/2pp1P2/3p4/3Q1N2/PPP1PP.text:
We'll play ...c5 and hold on to the d4-pawn for now, creating a strong center.

Next, we'll develop in a standard manner; get the knight to c6 to defend the center and try to capture on f5.

If White plays Bh3 to defend the f5-pawn, we can go for ...Ne7 and attack it one more time!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p1P2/3P4/8/PPP1PP1P.text:
If White captures on f5, they've just made our life easier.

We'll simply recapture and develop a piece at the same time.

We've got excellent control of the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p1p2/2PP4/3Q4/PP2PP.text:
Another possibility is to challenge the center right away with c4.

But, as in the 2.g4 lines, we won't budge.

We'll protect the center and open up the dark-squared bishop.

In this line, I recommend the best approach to be turning our style of play into a Stonewall.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p1p2/3P2P1/3Q4/PPP1.text:
After playing Qd3, 3.g4 is the most popular move, played about 44% of the time, called the Manhattan gambit.

White wants to put maximum pressure on our f5-pawn, and the natural continuations would be ...e6 or ...g6 to defend the pawn.

But we'll go for ...e5, as we want to initiate some trades in the center and make it easier for our pieces to develop!

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p1p2/3P4/2NQ4/PPP1P.text:
Instead of challenging the center with c4, White might try to put pressure on it with the knight on c3.

The idea is to get the queenside pieces out fast and castle long.

That just allows us to develop the knight to f6 and defend the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/3p1pP1/3P4/8/PPP1PP1.text:
If White goes for g5, they've just moved the g-pawn two times in the opening.

Yes, we can't develop our knight to f6, but we'll get a lead in development.

Let's challenge the center right away with ...c5.

If White captures, we'll get to play ...e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/4p3/3p1p2/2PP4/3Q1N2/PP2.text:
White activates the knight to f3 and takes control of the e5-square.

We'll do the same with our kingside knight, seizing control of the e4-square!

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3p1P2/3Q4/8/PPP1PP1P/R.text:
Many players will recapture here, as it is the most logical move.

We'll activate the knight with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3p1P2/3p4/3Q1N2/PPP1PP.text:
Instead of capturing right away, White might want to develop and prepare to recapture with the knight.

Well, we won't let them!

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pPp2/6P1/3Q4/PPP1PP1P.text:
If White captures on e5, we'll go for that pawn straight away.

Our knight develops to c6 and attacks the pawn.

White can't really play f4 to defend, as that would weaken the h4-d1 diagonal too much.

If White plays Bf4, ...g5 is a good move.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3ppP2/3P4/3Q4/PPP1PP1P.text:
Capturing on f5 doesn't pose us any problems whatsoever.

We've accomplished placing two pawns in the center.

Now, we'll disrupt White's center and make them move the queen once again, so that we can develop with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/3P2P1/8/PPP1PP1P.text:
The peculiar-looking 2.g4 by White is already challenging the f5-pawn we just placed in the center.

The idea is e4.
